title: WHAT IF YOU READ A STAR'S
FINAL HOURS IN DUST?

sets.star: Cross-section of a massive star, centred, filling most of the frame. Deep-navy bg with faint stars; concentric outlined shells like an onion, outermost pale blue (hydrogen), then cream (helium), then warm grey (carbon), then orange (oxygen), then purple (silicon), and a small dark-grey iron core, 4 px outlines, soft glow; setp.shells 0..1 = the shells draw on from the outside in; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera drift and gentle shimmer; setp.churn 0..1 = the carbon and oxygen shells wobble and swirl; setp.merge 0..1 = the carbon and oxygen shells blur into one orange-grey band; setp.collapse 0..1 = the core shrinks to a point, then at 1 a bright white flash; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.blast: A supernova explosion. Deep-navy bg; a white-gold shock ring expanding from the centre with orange and green filaments streaking outward and sparkling debris; setp.t 0..1 = the ring expands from small to the whole frame; setp.dust 0..1 = tiny grains appear in the cooling debris; setp.glow 'gold'|'red'|'cyan'.
sets.remnant: The supernova remnant Cassiopeia A. Black space bg; a roughly circular cloud of orange and green smoky filaments with light-blue pockets, ring-shaped dense orange band between centre and edge, drawn in the brand stylised look, 4 px outlines on the biggest wisps; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.zoom 0..1 = the camera pushes into the orange ring; setp.regions 0..3 = cream boxes labelled P1, P2 (GREEN MONSTER), P3 appear one by one; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.webbview: Webb observing screen. Deep-navy bg; a big outlined monitor with a glowing remnant image on the left half and a coloured spectrum graph on the right half with a thin baseline and labelled axes; setp.t 0..1 = slow push in; setp.spec 0..1 = the spectrum curve draws on; setp.pick 0..3 = a cream marker lands on peak 1 (SILICA), 2 (MAGNESIUM SILICATE), 3 (CARBON); setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.clumps: Dust clumps. Deep-navy bg; big soft dust clumps in cream-pink, charcoal and green drifting like smoke with tiny faceted grains sparkling inside; a small outlined Sun-and-planets solar system sits beside one clump for scale; setp.t 0..1 = drift; setp.size 0..1 = the solar system outline pulses next to a clump and a cream bracket 'AS BIG AS OUR SOLAR SYSTEM' appears; setp.type 'silica'|'carbon'|'mag' tints the clump colours; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.clock: A huge countdown clock. Deep-navy bg; a big outlined clock face centred with 12 hour ticks and a red sweeping hand and a red arc showing remaining time; setp.h 0..12 = hours left on the arc (the arc shrinks as it falls); setp.t 0..1 = hand sweeps; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red'.
sets.cycle: Cosmic recycling loop. Deep-navy bg; four outlined stations around a loop of gold arrows: an exploding star, a drifting cloud, a glowing new star with a tiny planet, and a tiny Earth-like ball; setp.t 0..1 = a gold pulse travels the loop; setp.stage 0..4 = stations light up one by one; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.timeline: A horizontal timeline. Deep-navy bg; a long gold line with milestone dots and cream calendar tags; setp.t 0..1 = the camera pans along the line; setp.now 0..1 = a bright cyan marker glides along; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props._probe_old: Icon of the BepiColombo stack: a small gold-foil box body with two dark solar-panel wings, a round grey antenna dish and a silver conical sunshield on top, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds an orange thruster flame at the bottom.
props.thermo: Tall outlined thermometer, cream glass tube, red or blue fluid to pp.frac (0..1), pp.label text beneath in FONTS.ui; pp.color red|cyan.
props.webb: Icon of the James Webb Space Telescope: a gold hexagon-segment mirror on a dark boom with a silver diamond sunshield below, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a soft gold bloom.
props.grain: A tiny outlined dust-grain crystal, faceted, 4 px outline; pp.type silica (cream-pink)|carbon (charcoal with grey highlights)|mag (green); pp.s scale; pp.glow true sparkles.
props.ironball: Small outlined dull-grey iron ball with a faint rust sheen and a tiny 'Fe' mark; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a red-orange heat bloom.
props.tag: Outlined cream tag on a short string with pp.text in FONTS.ui (max 12 chars); pp.color gold|cyan|red sets the string and underline.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back, arms loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation across the shot while looking around.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point up at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

chapters.sub: Dust the size of a solar system

chapters.title: THE CLUE
chapters.sub: Read the dust, read the star

film.vo: Hours before this star exploded, its insides got scrambled.
We can tell, because the dust it left behind kept the evidence.
This is Cassiopeia A, eleven thousand light-years away.
And Webb just read its dust, clump by clump.
What it found changes the last hours of a star's life.
So what if you could ride along for those final hours?
First, meet the star. It is huge, and built like an onion.
Not an onion you cry over. An onion you could not survive.
On the outside, hydrogen. Under it, helium.
Deeper still, carbon, then oxygen.
Every layer is burning one fuel into the next.
At the very middle, the burning stops at iron.
Iron is a dead end. Nothing more can be squeezed out of it.
Those shells are a diary. Every layer is a chapter of its life.
Remember the oxygen and carbon layers. They matter in a moment.
Because inside, something is about to go wrong.
The star is in its last hours, and the layers are churning.
Hot material rises and falls, stirring the boundaries between shells.
Then the wall between the carbon and oxygen layers gives way.
Scientists call it a shell merger.
Two layers blend into one, and the star changes its own shape.
That changes which elements get thrown out when it blows.
Here is the catch. You cannot see any of this from outside.
A star hides its insides, right up to the end.
So how can anyone know it happened hours before?
Hold that thought. First, the boom.
The iron core cannot hold. Gravity wins.
It collapses to a point, and the whole star rebounds.
A shock wave rips outward and throws the layers across space.
Hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen, scattered like confetti.
But the explosion is not the end of the story.
Light from this blast reached Earth around sixteen sixty-seven.
And the wreckage is still glowing today.
That wreckage is Cassiopeia A.
It is the leftover of the star you just watched die.
In the cooling debris, something new appears: dust.
Tiny grains of silica, carbon and magnesium silicate.
Each type forms in a different layer of the dead star.
So the dust remembers which layer it came from.
The grains clump together, in blobs as big as our solar system.
Each clump is a sealed time capsule, drifting out there.
Which clump came from the merged layers? Good question.
To find out, you would need a very sharp pair of eyes.
Lucky for us, we now have a telescope built for exactly this.
The James Webb Space Telescope. Its mid-infrared camera sees warm dust glow.
First, the team needed clues about where to look.
Old data from the retired Spitzer telescope pointed to three regions.
Webb split the light from each one into a spectrum.
A spectrum is like a barcode. Each kind of dust has its own.
Region one is full of silica, glass-like grains.
Region two glows with magnesium silicates.
That one is the Green Monster, a structure Webb found itself.
But it is not from the explosion. The star shed it earlier.
Region three is mostly carbon, in two neon-rich crescents.
Silica here, carbon there. Different layers, different dust.
Now for the big question. Could those layers have mixed?
The team compared the dust with models of exploding stars.
Only a carbon and oxygen merger explains what they saw.
The signs are not in one spot. They span much of the remnant.
Add X-ray data from Chandra and Japan's XRISM.
Together they say the merger was underway very shortly before the explosion.
A scientist said, we think it shows the hours before collapse.
Notice the wording. We think. Even NASA stays careful.
Nobody saw the star's last hours. The dust is a witness.
Hundreds of years later, we can still read it.
It is forensics, across eleven thousand light-years.
It is a best reading, not a video of the moment.
X-rays and dust agree on the merger. That makes it strong.
Why does a star's last few hours matter to you?
Because the blast decides which elements fly out.
That mix seeds the next generation of stars and planets.
Your own world was built from dust like this.
The oxygen you are breathing was cooked in a star.
And now there is a new tool for reading any supernova remnant.
Other astronomers can use it to peek inside other dead stars.
So the next time you look up, remember the onion.
So back to the star, and its scrambled insides.
Nobody can ride along. But the dust did.
It kept a note of what happened inside.
Webb just learned to read it.
Which layer of a star would you want to see first?
Tell me in the comments.
Tomorrow: what if the Moon got its own nuclear reactor?

short.vo: Hours before this star exploded, its insides got scrambled.
A star is built like an onion, with burning layers.
In its last hours, the carbon and oxygen layers merged.
Then the iron core collapsed and the star blew apart.
The wreckage is Cassiopeia A, eleven thousand light-years away.
Its dust clumps are as big as our solar system.
Webb read that dust, and the chemistry points to the merger.
Silica in one region, carbon in another. Different layers.
NASA says the mixing came very shortly before the blast.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: a nuclear reactor on the Moon.
